diagram_classification: Cosmological / geographical (probable): a schematic circular world or cosmos diagram, possibly a zonal or wind diagram. This is a tentative classification because the image contains no legible labels.
interpretation: The diagram shows a series of concentric circles. A small central circle has a dotted ring. Around it is a broad blank band, and outside that is a ring divided into compartments by paired radial lines. The outer ring appears to hold about eight to twelve sectors, with a few more visible at the top and bottom. The most likely reading is a schematic of the world or cosmos. The central disc would be the earth, or the terrestrial sphere, and the dotted ring would be the encircling ocean or a boundary of the inhabited world. The wide band would be the surrounding ocean, the aerial or elemental region, or the spheres. The outer ring of radial compartments would be divisions of the heavens, such as winds, months, zodiacal signs or hours, which are commonly arranged in this way. The ring could also be a computistical or calendrical wheel with its compartments left unlabelled. No inscriptions are legible, so the specific content of the sectors is uninterpreted.
evidence: Visible: concentric circles drawn in red and brown ink; a small central circle bordered by a dotted ring; a wide empty annulus; an outer ring divided into rectangular compartments by paired radial lines; and partial marginal text and other roundels at the edges of the page. The divisions are regular, which suggests a symmetrical scheme such as winds, months or zodiacal sectors. External: medieval diagrams of the earth, the spheres, the winds and the calendar often use concentric rings with radial subdivisions. Because no labels or figures can be read, the identification of the sectors and rings is uninterpreted and the certainty is low.
